As he interpreted to them, so it happened to them, and Pharaoh restored the chief butler to his office, and killed the chief baker, as Joseph had interpreted to them.
But the chief butler forgot Joseph in the prison, although he had told him what would happen to him, and he did not remember to tell Pharaoh how Joseph had told him, for he forgot.

notes.text: “Chief cook” renders the Greek of Gen 37:36; the Hebrew means “captain of the guard.” See 34:11.

chapters.heading: Joseph in Potiphar’s House and in Prison

verses.text: In those days Pharaoh dreamed two dreams in one night concerning a famine that was to come over all the land, and he woke from his sleep and called all the interpreters of dreams in Egypt and the magicians, and told them his two dreams, and they were not able to explain them.
Then the chief butler remembered Joseph and spoke of him to the king, and he brought him out of the prison, and he told his two dreams before him.

He told Pharaoh that the two dreams were a single dream, and he said, “Seven years of abundance are coming over the whole land of Egypt, and after them seven years of famine, a famine unlike any the land has known.

Let Pharaoh now name officials across Egypt to collect and store grain in every town during the years of plenty. Then there will be food for the seven years of famine, and the country will not perish in the famine, which will be extremely harsh.”
The Lord gave Joseph favor and mercy in Pharaoh’s eyes, and Pharaoh said to his servants, “We will not find such a wise and discerning man as this man, for the spirit of the Lord is with him.”
He appointed him second in all his kingdom and gave him authority over all Egypt, and had him ride in Pharaoh’s second chariot.

He clothed him with linen garments and put a gold chain on his neck, and a herald proclaimed before him, “’El ’El wa ’Abirer,” and he put a ring on his hand and made him ruler over all his house, and magnified him, and said to him: “Only on the throne will I be greater than you.”{a}

Joseph governed all of Egypt. Pharaoh’s officials, his servants, and everyone who handled the king’s business loved him, because he behaved with integrity, free of pride and arrogance, showing no favoritism and accepting no bribes, and judged all the people of the land fairly.

Egypt enjoyed peace under Pharaoh because of Joseph. The Lord was with him and gave him favor and kindness throughout his life among everyone who knew him or heard of him, and Pharaoh’s realm was well governed. There was no Satan and no wicked person in it.{b}
The king called Joseph’s name Sephantiphans, and gave Joseph as wife the daughter of Potiphar, daughter of the priest of Heliopolis, the chief cook.{c}
On the day Joseph stood before Pharaoh he was thirty years old.

In that year Isaac died. And as Joseph had said in the interpretation of the two dreams, there were seven years of plenty over all the land of Egypt, and the land of Egypt produced abundantly, one measure yielding eighteen hundred measures.
Joseph gathered food into every city until they were full of grain, until they could no longer count and measure it for its great quantity.

notes.text: “’El ’El wa ’Abirer” probably reflects Hebrew ’el ’el wa-’abir ’el, “God, God, and the mighty one of God,” an expansion of the Hebrew word abrek (“bow the knee”) in Gen 41:43. “Mighty one of God” may be a title of a great magician; compare Acts 8:10.
The absence of Satan is a sign of great happiness; compare 23:29.

Sephantiphans is Zaphenath-paneah (Gen 41:45). The author treats Potiphar of Gen 37:36 and Potiphera of Gen 41:45 as one man. Later Jewish legend makes Asenath a daughter of Dinah raised in his house.

chapters.heading: Pharaoh’s Dreams and Joseph’s Rise

verses.text: In the second year of the second week of the forty-fifth jubilee, Judah chose a wife for his firstborn Er from the daughters of Aram, a woman named Tamar.{a}
Er detested her and did not sleep with her, because his own mother was a Canaanite woman and he wanted a wife from his mother’s family, but his father Judah would not permit it.
This Er, Judah’s firstborn, was wicked, and the Lord killed him.
Judah said to his brother Onan, “Go in to your brother’s wife and do a husband’s brother’s duty to her, and raise up offspring for your brother.”

Onan knew that the offspring would not be his, but his brother’s only, and he went into his brother’s wife’s house and spilled the seed on the ground; and he was wicked in the Lord’s eyes, and he killed him.
Judah said to Tamar, his daughter-in-law, “Stay in your father’s house as a widow until my son Shelah grows up, and I will give you to him as a wife.”
He grew up; but Bedsu’el, Judah’s wife, did not allow her son Shelah to marry. And Bedsu’el, Judah’s wife, died in the fifth year of this week.{b}
In the sixth year Judah went up to shear his sheep at Timnah. They told Tamar, “Look, your father-in-law is going up to Timnah to shear his sheep.”{c}
She took off her widow’s clothing, put on a veil, made herself up, and sat at the town gate by the road to Timnah.
As Judah was going along he found her and thought she was a prostitute, and he said to her, “Let me come in to you”; and she said to him, “Come in,” and he went in.
She said to him, “Give me my pay”; and he said to her, “I have nothing in my hand but my ring on my finger, and my necklace, and the staff in my hand.”
She said to him, “Give them to me until you send me my pay”; and he said to her, “I will send you a kid from the goats”; and he gave them to her, and went in to her, and she conceived by him.
Judah went to his sheep, and she went to her father’s house.
Judah sent a young goat by his shepherd, an Adullamite, but the man could not find her. He asked the locals, “Where is the prostitute who was here?” They answered, “We have no prostitute here.”

He returned and told him that he had not found her: “I asked the people of the place, and they said to me, ‘There is no prostitute here.’” He said, “Let her keep them, or we will become a laughingstock.”
When she had completed three months, it was plain that she was pregnant, and they told Judah, “Look, your daughter-in-law Tamar is pregnant by prostitution.”
Judah went to her father’s house and said to her father and her brothers, “Bring her out and let them burn her, for she has done an unclean thing in Israel.”{d}
When they brought her out to burn her, she sent the ring, the necklace, and the staff to her father-in-law, saying, “Recognize whose these are, for by him I am pregnant.”
Judah recognized them and said, “Tamar is more righteous than I am. Therefore let them not burn her.”
For that reason she was not given to Shelah, and he did not approach her again.
After that she bore two sons, Perez and Zerah, in the seventh year of this second week.{e}
With that, the seven years of fruitfulness of which Joseph spoke to Pharaoh were completed.

Judah admitted that what he had done was wrong, since he had slept with his daughter-in-law. He found it repulsive and conceded that he had sinned and gone astray, having exposed his own son’s robe. He began to lament and plead with the Lord for his offense.
We told him in a dream that it was forgiven him because he pleaded earnestly and lamented and did not do it again.

He received forgiveness because he turned from his sin and from his ignorance, for he had transgressed greatly before our God; and everyone who acts in this way, everyone who lies with his mother-in-law, let them burn him with fire, so that he burns in it, for uncleanness and pollution are on them; let them burn them with fire.{f}

And you, command the children of Israel that there be no uncleanness among them, for everyone who lies with his daughter-in-law or with his mother-in-law has committed uncleanness; let them burn the man who lay with her with fire, and likewise the woman, and he will turn wrath and punishment away from Israel.{g}
To Judah we declared that his two sons had not slept with her, and for that reason his line was kept going into a second generation and would not be uprooted.
For in singleness of eye he had gone and sought punishment, namely according to the judgment of Abraham, which he had commanded his sons: Judah had sought to burn her with fire.{h}

notes.text: Year 2165 from creation in Charles’s count. Testament of Judah 10 says “from Mesopotamia.”
Bedsu’el is Bathshua; see 34:20.
Year 2168 from creation in Charles’s count.
Burning was the penalty for a priest’s daughter (Lev 21:9); the Targum Pseudo-Jonathan says Tamar was a priest’s daughter. Compare 30:7.
Year 2170 from creation in Charles’s count.
Compare Lev 20:14.
Compare Lev 18:15; 20:12, which do not specify the manner of death; Gen 38:24 presupposes burning.

chapters.heading: Judah and Tamar

verses.text: In the first year of the third week of the forty-fifth jubilee, famine began to settle on the land; the rain refused to fall at all.{a}
The earth turned barren, yet in Egypt there was food, since Joseph had gathered grain in the seven years of plenty and kept it safe.
The Egyptians came to Joseph for him to give them food, and he opened the storehouses where the grain of the first year was, and sold it to the people of the land for gold.

The famine was terribly severe in Canaan. Jacob heard there was grain in Egypt and sent his ten sons there to buy some for him. He did not send Benjamin, and Jacob’s ten sons reached Egypt together with the others who had come.

Joseph recognized them, but they did not recognize him, and he spoke to them and questioned them, and said to them, “Are you not spies, and have you not come to explore the approaches of the land?” And he put them in custody.
After that he set them free again, and held Simeon alone and sent his nine brothers away.
He filled their sacks with grain, and put their gold in their sacks, and they did not know.
He commanded them to bring their younger brother, for they had told him that their father was living, and their younger brother.

They went up from the land of Egypt and came to the land of Canaan, and told their father all that had happened to them and how the lord of the country had spoken harshly to them and had seized Simeon until they should bring Benjamin.
Jacob said, “You have bereaved me of my children! Joseph is gone and Simeon is gone too, and you will take Benjamin away. Your wickedness has come on me.”{b}

He said, “My son will not go down with you, in case he falls sick; for their mother bore two sons, and one has perished, and you will take this one from me too. If he were to catch a fever on the road, you would bring my old age down with sorrow to death.”{c}
For he saw that their money had been returned to each man in his sack, and for this reason he was afraid to send him.

The famine increased and became severe in the land of Canaan and in all lands except the land of Egypt, for many of the Egyptians had stored up their seed for food from the time they saw Joseph gathering seed together and putting it in storehouses and keeping it for the years of famine.
The people of Egypt fed themselves on it during the first year of their famine.
But when Israel saw that the famine was very severe in the land and there was no relief, he said to his sons, “Go again and get food for us so that we do not die.”
They said, “We will not go; unless our youngest brother goes with us, we will not go.”
Israel saw that if he did not send him with them, they would all perish because of the famine.
Reuben said, “Hand him over to me. If I do not bring him back to you, put my two sons to death in place of his life.” Jacob answered, “He will not go with you.”
Judah stepped forward and said, “Send him with me. If I do not bring him back, let the blame rest on me before you for the rest of my days.”
He sent him along with them in the second year of this week, on the first of the month. They reached Egypt with the other travelers, carrying gifts: balm, almonds, terebinth nuts, and pure honey.{d}

They went and stood before Joseph, and he saw his brother Benjamin and knew him, and said to them, “Is this your youngest brother?” They said to him, “It is he.” He said, “May the Lord be gracious to you, my son!”
He sent him into his house and brought Simeon out to them, and made a feast for them, and they presented to him the gift they had brought in their hands.
They ate before him, and he gave them all a portion, but Benjamin’s portion was seven times larger than any of theirs.
They ate and drank and got up and stayed with their donkeys.

Joseph devised a plan to learn their thoughts, whether thoughts of peace prevailed among them, and he said to the steward over his house, “Fill all their sacks with food, and return their money to them in their containers, and put my cup, the silver cup I drink from, in the sack of the youngest, and send them away.”

notes.text: Year 2171 from creation in Charles’s count.
This interprets Gen 42:36, “All this is against me.”
Compare Gen 42:38: “if harm befalls him on the journey.”
Year 2172 from creation in Charles’s count. The month is not named.

chapters.heading: The Brothers’ Two Journeys to Egypt

verses.text: He did as Joseph had instructed, filling all their sacks with grain, returning each man’s money into his sack, and placing the cup in Benjamin’s sack.

Early in the morning they left, and when they had gone from there, Joseph said to the steward of his house, “Pursue them, run and seize them, saying, ‘You have repaid me evil for good; you have stolen from me the silver cup from which my lord drinks.’ And bring their youngest brother back to me, and bring him quickly before I go out to my seat of judgment.”
He ran after them and said these words to them.

They said to him, “God forbid that your servants should do this thing and steal any vessel from your lord’s house, when the money we found in our sacks the first time we, your servants, brought back from the land of Canaan.
How then should we steal any vessel? Look, here we are with our sacks; search, and wherever you find the cup in the sack of any of us, let him be killed, and we and our donkeys will serve your lord.”
He said to them, “Not so; the man with whom I find it, only he will I take as a servant, and you will return in peace to your house.”
As he searched their containers, beginning with the eldest and ending with the youngest, it was found in Benjamin’s sack.
They tore their clothes and loaded their donkeys and returned to the city and came to Joseph’s house, and they all bowed down on their faces to the ground before him.

Joseph said to them, “You have done evil.” They said, “What shall we say and how shall we defend ourselves? Our lord has discovered the transgression of his servants; look, we are our lord’s servants, and our donkeys too.”

Joseph said to them, “I also fear the Lord. As for you, go to your homes and let your brother be my servant, for you have done evil. Do you not know that a man delights in his cup as I do in this cup? And yet you have stolen it from me.”{a}

Judah said, “O my lord, let your servant, I pray, speak a word in my lord’s ear: your servant’s mother bore two sons to our father; one went away and was lost and has not been found, and he alone is left of his mother, and our father, your servant, loves him, and his life is bound up with this boy’s life.
When we go to your servant our father and the boy is not with us, he will die, and we will bring our father down with sorrow to death.

Now let me, your servant, stay in place of the boy as a slave to my lord, and let the boy go with his brothers, for I became surety for him from the hand of your servant our father, and if I do not bring him back, your servant will bear the blame before our father forever.”
Joseph saw that they were all of one mind in goodness toward each other, and he could not control himself, and he told them that he was Joseph.
He spoke with them in the Hebrew language and fell on their necks and wept. But they did not recognize him, and they began to weep.{b}
He said to them, “Do not weep over me, but hurry and bring my father to me; and you see that it is my mouth that speaks and the eyes of my brother Benjamin that see.
This is only the second year of the famine, and five more years remain with no harvest, no fruit on the trees, and no plowing.

Come down quickly, you and your households, so that you do not perish through the famine, and do not grieve over your possessions, for the Lord sent me before you to set things in order so that many people might live.
Tell my father that I am alive. See, you can tell him the Lord has made me a father to Pharaoh and master of his house and of the whole country of Egypt.
Tell my father of all my glory and all the riches and glory the Lord has given me.”
By the command of Pharaoh’s mouth he gave them chariots and provisions for the way, and gave them all many-colored clothing and silver.
To their father he sent clothing and silver and ten donkeys carrying grain, and he sent them away.
They went up and told their father that Joseph was alive, that he was measuring out grain to all the nations of the world, and that he ruled all of Egypt.

Their father could not believe it, for he was out of his mind with shock. But when he saw the wagons Joseph had sent, his spirit came back to life. He said, “It is enough for me that Joseph lives. I will go down to see him before I die.”

notes.text: Compare Gen 44:15, “Do you not know that a man like me can divine?” The change in Jubilees may be deliberate.
That Joseph spoke Hebrew is a Midrashic touch; compare Genesis Rabbah 93.

chapters.heading: Joseph Makes Himself Known

verses.text: Israel left his home on the first of the third month, traveled by way of the Well of the Oath, and on the seventh of that month offered a sacrifice to the God of his father Isaac.{a}
Jacob remembered the dream he had seen at Bethel, and he was afraid to go down to Egypt.
He was considering sending word to Joseph to come to him, since he himself did not wish to go down. So he waited there seven days, in case a vision might show him whether to stay or to go down.

He celebrated the harvest feast of first fruits with old grain, because in all Canaan there was not a handful of seed; the famine had struck the wild animals, the livestock, and the birds, as well as human beings.{b}

On the sixteenth the Lord appeared to him and said to him, “Jacob, Jacob.” He said, “Here I am.” He said to him, “I am the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham and Isaac; do not be afraid to go down to Egypt, for I will make a great nation of you there.{c}
I will go down with you, and I will bring you up again, and in this land you will be buried, and Joseph will close your eyes with his hands. Do not be afraid; go down to Egypt.”
His sons and his sons’ sons got up and put their father and their possessions on wagons.
Israel left the Well of the Oath on the sixteenth of this third month and went to the land of Egypt.
Israel sent Judah ahead of him to his son Joseph to survey the land of Goshen, for Joseph had told his brothers to come and live there so they might be near him.
This was the best land in the land of Egypt, and near him, for all of them and for the cattle too.
These are the names of the sons of Jacob who went to Egypt with their father Jacob.{d}
Reuben, the firstborn of Israel; and these are the names of his sons: Enoch, Pallu, Hezron, and Carmi — five, counting the father.
Simeon and his sons; and these are the names of his sons: Jemuel, Jamin, Ohad, Jachin, Zohar, and Shaul, son of the Zephathite woman — seven.{e}
Levi and his sons; and these are the names of his sons: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari — four.
Judah and his sons; and these are the names of his sons: Shelah, Perez, and Zerah — four.
Issachar and his sons; and these are the names of his sons: Tola, Phua, Jasub, and Shimron — five.
Zebulun and his sons; and these are the names of his sons: Sered, Elon, and Jahleel — four.

These are the sons of Jacob, and their sons, born to him by Leah in Mesopotamia: six sons, and one sister, Dinah. All the persons descended from Leah who went to Egypt with their father Jacob numbered twenty-nine; counting their father Jacob, thirty.
The sons of Zilpah, Leah’s servant, wife of Jacob, whom she bore to Jacob: Gad and Asher.
These are the names of their sons who went with him to Egypt: the sons of Gad: Ziphion, Haggi, Shuni, Ezbon, Eri, Areli, and Arodi — eight.
The sons of Asher: Imnah, Ishvah, Ishvi, Beriah, and Serah, their one sister — six.
All the souls were fourteen, and all those of Leah were forty-four.
The sons of Rachel, wife of Jacob: Joseph and Benjamin.
To Joseph in Egypt, before his father came to Egypt, were born those whom Asenath, daughter of Potiphar, priest of Heliopolis, bore to him: Manasseh and Ephraim — three.
The sons of Benjamin: Bela, Becher, Ashbel, Gera, Naaman, Ehi, Rosh, Muppim, Huppim, and Ard — eleven.
All the souls of Rachel were fourteen.
The sons of Bilhah, the servant of Rachel, wife of Jacob, whom she bore to Jacob, were Dan and Naphtali.
These are the names of their sons who went with them to Egypt. The sons of Dan were Hushim, Samon, Asudi, ’Ijaka, and Salomon — six.
They died in the year in which they entered Egypt, and Hushim alone was left to Dan.{f}
These are the names of the sons of Naphtali: Jahziel, Guni, Jezer, Shallum, and ’Iv.{g}
And ’Iv, who was born after the years of famine, died in Egypt.
All the souls of Rachel were twenty-six.
All the souls of Jacob who went to Egypt were seventy souls. These are his children and his children’s children, seventy in all; but five died in Egypt before Joseph and had no children.
In Canaan two of Judah’s sons, Er and Onan, died childless. The Israelites buried those who died there, and they were counted among the seventy nations.

notes.text: First of month 3 is about May 21, and the seventh about May 27, in the book’s 364-day calendar. The Ethiopic here reads “Haran” for the starting place, which is probably corrupt for Hebron; compare Gen 37:14. The Well of the Oath is Beersheba.
The Feast of Weeks, the fifteenth of month 3 (about June 4). See Gen 46:1.
The sixteenth is about June 5.

The total of seventy includes Jacob himself. Another count, in Exod 1:5, reaches seventy by leaving Jacob out; Acts 7:14 has seventy-five, following the Greek. The lists below differ in places from Genesis 46, and the tallies in the Ethiopic text do not always add up.
“Zephathite” means a native of the Canaanite city Zephath; compare Judg 1:17.
Genesis 46:23 mentions Hushim alone.
Neither Gen 46:24 nor 1 Chron 7:13 has ’Iv.

chapters.heading: Jacob Goes Down to Egypt

verses.text: On the first of the fourth month, in the second year of the third week of the forty-fifth jubilee, Israel entered Egypt, in the region of Goshen.{a}
Joseph went to meet his father Jacob in the land of Goshen, and fell on his father’s neck and wept.
Israel said to Joseph, “Now I can die, having seen you. Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, the God of Abraham and of Isaac, who has not held back his kindness and favor from his servant Jacob.
It is enough for me that I have seen your face while I am still alive; yes, the vision I saw at Bethel is true. Blessed be the Lord my God forever and ever, and blessed be his name.”

Joseph and his brothers ate and drank in their father’s presence. Jacob was overjoyed to see Joseph eating and drinking with his brothers in front of him, and he blessed the Maker of all things, who had kept him alive and kept all twelve of his sons for him.

Joseph gave his father and brothers, as a grant, the right to settle in Goshen, in Rameses, and in the whole surrounding district under his authority beneath Pharaoh. Israel and his sons lived in Goshen, the finest part of Egypt. Israel was a hundred and thirty years old when he arrived in Egypt.
Joseph supported his father and his brothers and also their possessions with as much bread as they needed for the seven years of the famine.
Egypt was devastated by the famine. In exchange for grain, Joseph acquired all the land of Egypt for Pharaoh, and took the people, their livestock, and everything else into Pharaoh’s possession.
The years of famine were completed, and Joseph gave the people in the land seed and food so they could sow the land in the eighth year, for the river had overflowed all the land of Egypt.

During the seven famine years the river had not flooded and had watered only a few spots along its banks. Now it rose over its banks, the Egyptians sowed their fields, and that year the ground yielded abundant grain.
This was the first year of the fourth week of the forty-fifth jubilee.{b}
Joseph took a fifth part of the grain of the harvest for the king and left four parts for them as food and seed, and Joseph made it an ordinance for the land of Egypt until this day.

Israel lived in the land of Egypt seventeen years, and all the days he lived were three jubilees, a hundred and forty-seven years, and he died in the fourth year of the fifth week of the forty-fifth jubilee.{c}

Israel blessed his sons before he died and told them everything that would happen to them in the land of Egypt; and he made known to them what would come on them in the last days, and blessed them, and gave Joseph two portions in the land.{d}
He died and joined his ancestors, and was buried in the twin cave in Canaan, beside his father Abraham, in the tomb he had dug for himself in the twin cave in the region of Hebron.
He gave all his books and the books of his fathers to his son Levi so that he might preserve them and renew them for his children until this day.{e}

notes.text: The first of month 4 is about June 21 in the 364-day calendar. Year 2172 from creation in Charles’s count.
Year 2178 from creation in Charles’s count.
3 × 49 = 147. Year 2188 from creation in Charles’s count.
Compare Gen 49 and 48:22.
The author presents the ancestral writings as kept by the priestly line of Levi.

chapters.heading: Jacob in Egypt and His Death

verses.text: After Jacob’s death the Israelites multiplied in Egypt and became a great nation. They were united in heart: brother loved brother, and each helped the other. They increased enormously for ten weeks of years, throughout Joseph’s lifetime.{a}
There was no Satan and no evil all the days of Joseph’s life that he lived after his father Jacob, for all the Egyptians honored the children of Israel all the days of Joseph’s life.
Joseph died aged one hundred ten. Seventeen of his years were spent in Canaan, ten as a slave, three in prison, and eighty serving the king as ruler of all Egypt.
He died, and all his brothers, and all that generation.
Before he died he ordered the Israelites to take his bones with them when they left Egypt.

He made them swear about his bones, for he knew that the Egyptians would not bring him out again and bury him in the land of Canaan, for Makamaron, king of Canaan, while living in the land of Assyria, fought in the valley with the king of Egypt and killed him there, and pursued the Egyptians to the gates of Ermon.{b}
He could not get in, because a different, newer king now ruled Egypt, a stronger man than he. So he went back to Canaan. The gates of Egypt were closed, and nobody left or entered.
Joseph died in the sixth week, second year, of the forty-sixth jubilee. He was buried in Egypt, and all his brothers died after him.{c}

In the second year of the second week of the forty-seventh jubilee, the king of Egypt marched to war against the king of Canaan. The Israelites carried out the bones of all Jacob’s sons except Joseph’s and buried them in the twin cave in the field on the mountain.{d}
Most of them returned to Egypt, but a few of them stayed in the mountains of Hebron, and your father Amram stayed with them.{e}
The king of Canaan was victorious over the king of Egypt, and he shut the gates of Egypt.
He devised an evil plan against the children of Israel, to afflict them; and he said to the people of Egypt,

“See how the Israelite people have grown more numerous and stronger than we are. Let us plan carefully against them before they multiply further, and wear them down with forced labor before war breaks out and they side against us. Otherwise they will join our enemies and leave our land, for their hearts and eyes are fixed on Canaan.”

He appointed taskmasters over them to wear them down with forced labor. They built strong cities for Pharaoh, Pithom and Raamses, and rebuilt every wall and fortification in Egypt’s cities that had collapsed.
They made them serve with harshness, and the more they dealt evilly with them, the more they increased and multiplied.
The people of Egypt loathed the children of Israel.

notes.text: Ten weeks of years is seventy years.

Makamaron is unidentified. Ermon is probably Heroonpolis, near the desert. Testament of Simeon 8 says the Egyptians guarded Joseph’s bones in the royal tombs, because sorcerers said that darkness would fall on Egypt if they left. The war between Egypt and Canaan here may reflect the campaigns of Rameses III.
Year 2242 from creation in Charles’s count.
Year 2263 from creation in Charles’s count.
The angel speaks to Moses. The remark implies that some Hebrews were already in Canaan before the exodus.

chapters.heading: Joseph’s Death and the Oppression of Israel

verses.text: In the seventh week, in the seventh year, in the forty-seventh jubilee, your father went out from the land of Canaan, and you were born in the fourth week, in the sixth year of it, in the forty-eighth jubilee; this was the time of tribulation for the children of Israel.{a}
Pharaoh, king of Egypt, issued an order about them that they should throw all their newborn male children into the river.
They threw them in for seven months, until the day you were born. Your mother hid you for three months, and they informed on her.

She made an ark for you and covered it with pitch and asphalt, and put it in the reeds on the bank of the river, and she put you in it seven days, and your mother came by night and nursed you, and by day Miriam, your sister, guarded you from the birds.
In those days Tharmuth, the daughter of Pharaoh, came to bathe in the river, and she heard your voice crying, and she told her maidens to bring you out, and they brought you to her.
She took you out of the ark, and she had compassion on you.
Your sister said to her, “Shall I go and call one of the Hebrew women to nurse this baby for you?” She said to her, “Go.”
She went and called your mother Jochebed, and she gave her wages, and she nursed you.

Afterward, when you had grown up, they brought you to the daughter of Pharaoh, and you became her son, and your father Amram taught you writing, and after you had completed three weeks they brought you into the royal court.{b}
You were three weeks of years at court, until you left the royal court and saw an Egyptian striking your friend, who was one of the children of Israel, and you killed him and hid him in the sand.{c}
On the second day you found two of the children of Israel quarreling, and you said to the one who was doing the wrong, “Why do you strike your brother?”
He was angry and indignant, and said, “Who made you a prince and a judge over us? Do you think to kill me as you killed the Egyptian yesterday?” And you were afraid and fled because of these words.

notes.text: The angel is speaking to Moses; “your father” is Amram. Years 2303 and 2330 from creation in Charles’s count.
Three weeks of years is twenty-one years.
Years 2351–2372 from creation in Charles’s count.

chapters.heading: The Birth and Early Life of Moses

verses.text: In the sixth year of the third week of the forty-ninth jubilee you left and lived in the land of Midian for five weeks and one year. You returned to Egypt in the second week, in the second year, in the fiftieth jubilee.{a}
You yourself know what he said to you on Mount Sinai, and what Prince Mastema wanted to do with you when you were returning to Egypt, on the way, when you met him at the lodging place.{b}
Did he not with all his power seek to kill you and rescue the Egyptians from your hand, when he saw that you had been sent to carry out judgment and vengeance on the Egyptians?{c}
I rescued you from his hand, and you performed the signs and wonders you were sent to perform in Egypt against Pharaoh and all his house, his servants and his people.

For Israel’s sake the Lord took great vengeance on them. He struck them with blood, frogs, lice, flies, and painful boils that broke out in sores; he struck their livestock dead; he sent hail that destroyed everything that grew, and locusts that ate what the hail left, and darkness, and the death of the firstborn of people and animals. On all their idols the Lord took vengeance and burned them with fire.{d}
Everything was sent through your hand, so that you would declare these things before they were done, and you spoke with the king of Egypt before all his servants and before his people.
Everything happened according to your words; ten great and terrible judgments came on the land of Egypt, so that you might carry out vengeance on it for Israel.
The Lord did everything for Israel’s sake and in keeping with his covenant, which he had made with Abraham, that he would take vengeance on them as they had brought them into bondage by force.
Prince Mastema stood against you and tried to throw you into Pharaoh’s hands, and he helped the Egyptian sorcerers, and they stood up and worked before you.
We allowed them to work the evils, but we did not allow the remedies to be worked by their hands.
The Lord struck them with malignant ulcers, and they were not able to stand, for we destroyed them so that they could not perform a single sign.

Despite all these signs and wonders, Prince Mastema was not put to shame, because he took courage and cried out to the Egyptians to pursue you with all the forces of the Egyptians, with their chariots and horses and all the hosts of the peoples of Egypt.
I stood between Egypt and Israel, and we saved Israel from Pharaoh and his people. The Lord led the Israelites through the middle of the sea as though across dry ground.

All the nations he sent to chase Israel, the Lord our God hurled into the middle of the sea, into the deep abyss below the Israelites, just as the Egyptians had thrown their children into the river. He took vengeance on a million of them, and a thousand strong, vigorous men were destroyed for one nursing infant of your people whom they had thrown into the river.{e}

On the fourteenth day, on the fifteenth, on the sixteenth, on the seventeenth, and on the eighteenth, Prince Mastema was bound and imprisoned behind the children of Israel so that he could not accuse them.{f}
On the nineteenth we let them loose so that they could help the Egyptians and pursue the children of Israel.{g}
He hardened their hearts and made them stubborn, and the plan was devised by the Lord our God, so that he might strike the Egyptians and throw them into the sea.

On the fourteenth we bound him so that he could not accuse the children of Israel on the day when they asked the Egyptians for vessels and garments, silver vessels, gold vessels, and bronze vessels, in order to plunder the Egyptians in return for the bondage in which they had forced them to serve.
We did not lead the children of Israel out of Egypt empty-handed.

notes.text: Years 2372 and 2410 from creation in Charles’s count; five weeks and one year is 36 years. Midian: Exod 2:15.
“Mastema” (“hostility”) is the chief of the evil spirits in this book. Here he takes the place of the Lord in Exod 4:24 (compare 17:16 above and 1 Chron 21:1 against 2 Sam 24:1).
Other readers say Moses had failed to circumcise his son (so Targum Pseudo-Jonathan on Exod 4:24); the explanation in Jubilees seems to be its author’s own.
This lists the ten plagues of Exod 7–12.
This is another case of measure-for-measure punishment; compare 4:31 and Wisdom 18:5.
In the 364-day calendar these days of month 1 fall about April 4–8.
About April 9.

chapters.heading: From Moses’ Flight to the Exodus

verses.text: Remember the commandment the Lord gave you about the Passover, that you should keep it in its season on the fourteenth of the first month, that you should kill it before evening, and that they should eat it by night, on the evening of the fifteenth, from the time of sunset.{a}

For on this night, the beginning of the festival and the beginning of the joy, you were eating the Passover in Egypt, when all the powers of Mastema had been let loose to kill all the firstborn in the land of Egypt, from the firstborn of Pharaoh to the firstborn of the captive woman at the mill, and the cattle.{b}

This is the sign the Lord gave them: they should not enter to kill any house on whose doorposts they saw the blood of a lamb of the first year, but should pass over it, so that all those in the house would be saved, because the sign of the blood was on its doorposts.

The Lord’s powers did everything as the Lord commanded them, and they passed over all the children of Israel, and the plague did not come on them to destroy any soul among them, whether of cattle, or people, or dog.
The plague struck Egypt with terrible force. Not one house in Egypt escaped a death, and the land was full of weeping and wailing.
All Israel was eating the Passover lamb’s flesh and drinking wine, praising, blessing, and thanking the Lord God of their fathers, ready to leave Egypt’s yoke and cruel slavery.{c}

Remember this day all the days of your life, and keep it from year to year all the days of your life, once a year, on its day, according to all its law, and do not put it off from day to day or from month to month.

For it is an eternal ordinance, engraved on the heavenly tablets concerning all the children of Israel, that they should keep it every year on its day, once a year, throughout all their generations; and there is no limit of days, for this is ordained forever.

Anyone who is clean, and nearby, yet fails to come and keep it on its day, bringing an acceptable offering before the Lord and eating and drinking in his presence at the festival, will be cut off. Since he did not bring the Lord’s offering at its set time, he will carry his own guilt.

Let the Israelites come and keep the Passover at its fixed time, on the fourteenth of the first month, in the twilight between the two evenings, from the third part of the day until the third part of the night. Two parts of the day belong to the light and the third part to the evening.{d}
This is what the Lord commanded you, that you should keep it between the evenings.

It is not permitted to kill it during any part of the daylight, but at the time bordering on the evening, and let them eat it in the evening until the third part of the night, and whatever is left of all its flesh from the third part of the night onward, let them burn with fire.{e}

They are not to cook it in water, nor to eat it raw, but roasted on the fire: they are to eat it with care, its head with its inner parts, and its feet, roasted with fire, and not break any bone of it; for no bone of the children of Israel is to be crushed.{f}

For this reason the Lord commanded the children of Israel to keep the Passover on the day of its fixed time, and not to break a bone of it; for it is a festival day and a commanded day, and there is to be no passing over from day to day or month to month, but let it be kept on the day of its festival.

Order the Israelites to keep the Passover every year of their lives, once yearly at its fixed time. It will serve as a remembrance that pleases the Lord, and in any year in which they observe the Passover in its season exactly as he commanded, no plague will come among them to kill or strike.
They are not to eat it outside the Lord’s sanctuary, but before the Lord’s sanctuary, and all the people of the congregation of Israel are to celebrate it in its appointed season.

Every man who has come on its day is to eat it in the sanctuary of your God before the Lord, from twenty years old and up; for so it is written and ordained that they should eat it in the Lord’s sanctuary.

When the children of Israel come into the land they are to possess, into the land of Canaan, and set up the Lord’s tabernacle in the middle of the land in one of their tribes until the Lord’s sanctuary has been built in the land, let them come and celebrate the Passover in the middle of the Lord’s tabernacle, and let them kill it before the Lord from year to year.
In the days when the house has been built in the Lord’s name in the land of their inheritance, they are to go there and kill the Passover in the evening, at sunset, at the third part of the day.

They are to offer its blood on the threshold of the altar and put its fat on the fire on the altar, and eat its flesh roasted with fire in the court of the house that has been sanctified in the Lord’s name.{g}
They may not celebrate the Passover in their cities, nor in any place except before the Lord’s tabernacle, or before his house where his name has dwelt; and they will not go astray from the Lord.

And you, Moses, order the Israelites to observe the Passover rules as you were commanded. Teach them every year the day of the festival, and the feast of unleavened bread, so that they eat unleavened bread for seven days, keep its festival, and each of those seven joyful days bring an offering before the Lord on your God’s altar.{h}
For you celebrated this festival in haste when you left Egypt, until you entered the wilderness of Shur; for on the shore of the sea you completed it.

notes.text: Month 1, day 14 is about April 4 in the 364-day calendar. The fourteenth, a Tuesday, begins at sunset the evening before.
In Exod 12:29 it is the Lord himself who strikes the firstborn.
This is the first mention of wine at the Passover meal. Later custom prescribes four cups; see Mishnah Pesahim 10.

The Jews divided the night into three watches, about 6–10 p.m., 10 p.m.–2 a.m., and 2–6 a.m.; the matching day-parts would be 6–10 a.m., 10 a.m.–2 p.m., and 2–6 p.m. This text says the last of these belongs to the evening. “Between the evenings” (Exod 12:6) was read by the Sadducees and Samaritans as between sunset and full dark, but by the Pharisees as the afternoon (about 3–6 p.m.).
The rabbis limited the eating to midnight.
The Latin, which is to be preferred, reads “There shall be no tribulation among the children of Israel on this day.” “With care” renders a Greek word; the Hebrew of Exod 12:11 is “in haste.”
In later times the lamb was killed in the Temple but eaten in houses in Jerusalem, because of the great numbers of pilgrims.
The Ethiopic is corrupt here; the Latin reads “during its days and during.”

chapters.heading: Rules for the Passover

verses.text: After this law I made known to you the days of the Sabbaths in the desert of Sin, which is between Elim and Sinai.{a}

I told you of the Sabbaths of the land on Mount Sinai, and I told you of the jubilee years in the sabbaths of years; but I have not told you the year of it until you enter the land you are to possess.{b}
The land too will keep its sabbaths while they live on it, and they will know the jubilee year.{c}

For this reason I have set out for you the year-weeks, the years, and the jubilees: there have been forty-nine jubilees from the days of Adam until this day, and one week and two years; and there are still forty years to come for learning the commandments of the Lord, until they cross over into the land of Canaan, crossing the Jordan to the west.{d}

The jubilees will pass by until Israel is cleansed from all guilt of fornication, uncleanness, pollution, sin, and error, and lives with confidence in all the land, and there will be no more Satan or any evil one, and the land will be clean from that time forever.{e}
Now look, the commandment about the Sabbaths: I have written it down for you, with all the judgments of its laws.

Six days you will labor, but the seventh day is the Sabbath of the Lord your God. On it you will do no work at all, you and your sons and your male servants and your female servants and all your cattle, and the foreigner who is with you.

The man who does any work on it will die; whoever desecrates that day, whoever lies with his wife, or whoever says he will do something on it, that he will set out on a journey on it for buying or selling; and whoever draws water on it that he had not prepared for himself on the sixth day, and whoever picks up any burden to carry it out of his tent or out of his house, will die.{f}

Do no work whatever on the Sabbath, other than what you made ready on the sixth day, so that you can eat, drink, rest, and refrain from all labor that day, and bless the Lord your God, who gave you a day of festival and a holy day. This day, among all their days, is a day of the holy kingdom for all Israel, forever.

For great is the honor the Lord has given to Israel, that they should eat, drink, and be satisfied on this festival day, and rest on it from all labor that belongs to the labor of human beings, except burning incense and bringing offerings and sacrifices before the Lord for days and for Sabbaths.

This work alone is to be done on the Sabbath days in the sanctuary of the Lord your God, so that they may atone for Israel with sacrifice continually from day to day, as a memorial pleasing before the Lord, and that he may receive them always from day to day as you have been commanded.{g}

Every man who does any work on it, or goes on a journey, or tills his farm, whether in his house or any other place, and whoever lights a fire, or rides on any animal, or travels by ship on the sea, and whoever strikes or kills anything, or slaughters a beast or a bird, or whoever catches an animal or a bird or a fish, or whoever fasts or makes war on the Sabbaths:{h}

the man who does any of these things on the Sabbath will die, so that the children of Israel may keep the Sabbaths according to the commandments about the Sabbaths of the land, as it is written on the tablets that he gave into my hands, so that I should write out for you the laws of the seasons and the seasons according to the division of their days. This completes the account of the division of the days.

notes.text: Exod 16:1.
The count is 49 × 49 + 7 + 2 = 2410 years from creation to the present moment in the story, with forty more years to the entry into Canaan, at 2450. A “year-week” is seven years.
This points to the messianic age; compare 1:29 and 23:26–30.

The rule against marital relations on the Sabbath is still followed by the Samaritans; the Mishnah teaches the opposite. Later rabbinic law allowed a journey of 2,000 cubits on the Sabbath (about 3,000 feet, a little over half a mile, or about 900 meters; the “Sabbath day’s journey” of Acts 1:12). Buying and selling were forbidden by Nehemiah (Neh 10:31; 13:15–22). Drawing water is forbidden by the Karaite Jews.
Compare Num 28:9–10 and Matt 12:5.

Fire is forbidden in Exod 35:3. Riding on an animal is forbidden by the oral law. In the Maccabean wars the rule against fighting was at first kept strictly (1 Macc 2:31–38) and then relaxed (1 Macc 2:41).
